  Terse gloss: "Head (body part); chief or leader; top or summit; military company; beginning; choicest portion; census total"
  Readable gloss: "One of the most frequent nouns in the Hebrew Bible, rosh fundamentally denotes the physical head of a person or animal but branches into a remarkably wide semantic range. Because the head is the topmost, foremost, and most prominent part of the body, it naturally extends to mean the top of a mountain, the chief of a tribe, the beginning of a period, and even the sum total of a census. These metaphorical extensions are ancient, attested across Semitic languages from Akkadian reshu to Arabic ra's to Ethiopic re's, and every major translation tradition reflects the branching: Spanish distinguishes cabeza from cima and principio, while Korean separates meori (head) from udumeori (leader) and kkokdaegi (summit)."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "head (anatomical)"
    Enriched: The literal, physical head of a human or animal — the default, unmarked sense appearing in roughly 57% of occurrences. Arabic ra's, Spanish cabeza, and German Haupt all converge on the anatomical meaning. Key passages include the baker's dream in Gen 40:20 and Jacob blessing Ephraim by placing his hand on the boy's head (Gen 48:14).
    Existing Spanish translations: cabecera-de, cabeza-de, de-la-casa-de-
  Sense 2: "chief, leader, head of group"
    Enriched: A chief, leader, or head of a clan, tribe, or administrative unit. The metaphor from body part to authority figure is pan-Semitic (Arabic ra'is, Swahili mkuu/kiongozi, Korean udumeori). Prominent in the genealogical registers of Chronicles (1 Chr 5:7, 5:24) where tribal leaders are enumerated by their headship.
    Existing Spanish translations: cabezas, cabezas-de
  Sense 3: "top, summit, peak"
    Enriched: The top, summit, or peak of a physical object — a mountain, pillar, tree, or tower. Korean kkokdaegi, Spanish cima/cumbre, and Swahili kilele all distinguish this spatial sense from the body-part meaning. Moses standing on the top of the hill with the staff of God (Exod 17:9-10) and the cloud covering Sinai's summit (Exod 19:20) are defining passages.
    Existing Spanish translations: a-la-cima-de, cabeza-de, cabeza-de-, cima-de, cumbre-de, cumbre-de-, la-cima-de, la-cumbre-de
  Sense 4: "chief, leader (metaphorical)"
    Enriched: A military company, division, or raiding band, typically in the plural. Judges 7:16 describes Gideon dividing three hundred men into three rashim (companies), and Judg 9:34-43 narrates Abimelech's tactical deployment of multiple bands. Arabic firaq, Korean budae, and Spanish divisiones confirm this specialized military sense.
    Existing Spanish translations: a-la-cabeza-de, a-la-cabeza-del, cabeza, cabeza-de, cabeza-de-, en-cabeza-de, entre-cabezas-de, la-cabeza, para-cabezas-de
  Sense 5: "company, division, band"

Judges 7:16 describes Gideon dividing three hundred men into three rashim (companies), and Judg 9:34-43 narrates Abimelech's tactical deployment of multiple bands. Arabic firaq, Korean budae, and Spanish divisiones confirm this specialized military sense.
    Existing Spanish translations: La-división, Y-la-división, cabezas, compañías, divisiones, escuadrones, las-cabezas, las-compañías, y-compañía-, y-la-división, y-las-compañías
  Sense 6: "beginning, first"
    Enriched: The beginning or first of a temporal or ordinal sequence. The head of time is its start: Prov 8:23 places Wisdom at the rosh of God's works, and Num 10:10 prescribes trumpet blasts at the rosh of months. Swahili mwanzo, Arabic bidaya, and Korean cheoeumbuteo all render this as 'beginning' rather than 'head.'
    Existing Spanish translations: Y-en-cabezas-de, al-principio, cabeza-de, desde-el-principio, desde-principio, y-en-principios-de, y-principio-de
  Sense 7: "chief, choicest, principal amount"
    Enriched: The choicest, finest, or principal quality of a substance, or the principal amount of a debt.     Existing Spanish translations: en-cabeza-de-él, en-principal-suyo
  Sense 8: "sum, total, census count"
    Enriched: The sum or total obtained by counting heads — a census figure. The idiom naso et rosh ('lift up the head') means 'take a census.' Ps 139:17 uses rosh for the sum of God's thoughts, and Ps 119:160 speaks of the sum (rosh) of God's word being truth. Swahili jumla and Korean hapgye both render this as 'total.'
    Existing Spanish translations: Suma-de, sus-sumas
